case_name: Gateway Building Management Limited v. Manjit Singh Randhawa
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Gateway Building Management Limited
v. Manjit Singh Randhawa,

2013 BCSC 350

Date: 20130307

Docket: S126910

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Gateway Building Management Limited and Kuldip Singh
Randhawa

Petitioners

And

Manjit Singh Randhawa, Conconi Ft. Holdings Limited,

Brian C. Markus Law Corporation, Brian C. Markus,

Lawson Lundell LLP, Craig C. Ferris, Laura Bevan, Kinji Bourchier

Respondents

AND:

Docket: S127699

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Gateway Building Management, Acumar Consulting

Engineers Limited and Kuldip Singh Randhawa

Plaintiffs

And

Manjit Singh Randhawa, Conconi Ft. Holdings Limited,

Brian C. Markus Law Corporation, Brian C. Markus,

Craig C. Ferris, Laura Bevan, Kinji Bourchier, Suzan El-Khatib

and S.E.K. Law Corporation Inc.

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice
Burnyeat

Reasons for Judgment

(from Chambers)

Appearing for Gateway Building
Management, Acumar Consulting Engineers Limited and Kuldip Singh Randhawa:

Kuldip Singh Randhawa

in person

Counsel for Brian C. Markus, Brian C. Markus
Law Corporation, Craig C. Ferris, Laura Bevan, Kinji Bourchier and Lawson
Lundell LLP:

B.D.M. Loewen

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver, B.C.

January 21, 23 and 24, 2013

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver, B.C.

March 7, 2013

[
1
]

Identical orders are sought in Action numbers S126910
(“Petition”) and S127699 (“Action”) by Brian C. Markus Law Corporation, Brian C.
Markus, Lawson Lundell LLP, Craig C. Ferris, Laura Bevan and Kinji Bourchier
(“Applicants”) that:  (a) the allegations made against the Applicants in
the October 2, 2012 Petition and in the November 1, 2012 Notice of
Civil Claim in the Action disclose no reasonable claim, are scandalous,
frivolous and vexatious, may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial of
the proceeding, or otherwise are an abuse of the process of the Honourable
Court; (b) the portions of the Petition and the Action that relate to the
Applicants be struck out; (c) the Applicants be entitled to Special Costs
against the Plaintiffs and the Petitioners; and (d) the Petitioners and
the Plaintiffs not advance or maintain any further legal proceedings against
the Applicants or their counsel without leave of the Court.

[
2
]

The applications are made pursuant to
Rule 9‑5 of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
, B.C. Reg. 168/2009,
and
s. 18
of the
Supreme Court Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 443.

BACKGROUND

[
3
]

Lawson Lundell LLP, Craig Ferris, Laura Bevan
and Kinji Bourchier act for Manjit Singh Randhawa (“Manjit”) in Supreme Court
of British Columbia Action Numbers S123329 and S111030.  Both of those actions
were commenced pursuant to s. 227 of the
Business Corporations Act
,
R.S.B.C. 2002, c. 57.  In Action S123329 (“Kuldip Oppression Action”)
it was alleged that Manjit through Gateway Building Management Ltd. (“Gateway”)
oppressed Kuldip Singh Randhawa (“Kuldip”).  The Kuldip Oppression Action has
been dismissed but that dismissal appealed.  Action S111030 (“Manjit
Oppression Action”) was commenced by Manjit against Gateway and Kuldip alleging
oppression.  No Reasons for Judgment have been issued relating to the
13 days of hearing required to hear the Manjit Oppression Action.  Counsel
in the Kuldip Oppression Action and the Manjit Oppression Action have been Ms. Bevan
and Mr. Bourchier throughout.

[
4
]

Brian C. Markus Law Corporation and Brian C.
Markus (collectively “Markus”) act for Conconi Ft. Holdings Limited (“Conconi”)
in Supreme Court of British Columbia Action No. H091177 (“Foreclosure
Action”).  A mortgage on the Property owned by Gateway was arranged by Kuldip
with Conconi (“Conconi Mortgage”).  The Conconi Mortgage replaced a mortgage
previously arranged by Kuldip.

[
5
]

After the Conconi Mortgage went into default,
foreclosure proceedings were commenced by Conconi, an Order
Nisi

foreclosure was obtained, and a six-month redemption period set.  Arrangements
were made between Conconi and Manjit to see the purchase of the Conconi
Mortgage by Manjit.  It has been the position taken throughout by Kuldip that
the Conconi Mortgage was redeemed by Manjit on behalf of Gateway, was not
purchased by Manjit in his own capacity, and that either it should be
discharged from title or a declaration should be made that nothing is owing
under it.  A number of rulings have been made to the effect that the Conconi
Mortgage was purchased and not redeemed.  Kuldip has not accepted those
rulings.  Those rulings are the subject of various appeals by Kuldip.

Claims against the Lawson Defendants

[
6
]

In the Action, the Plaintiffs state that Manjit
retained Lawson Lundell (specifically Messrs. Ferris and Bourchier and
Ms. Bevan).  The Plaintiffs refer to all four of those Defendants as the
“Lawson Defendants”.  The following allegations are made against the Lawson
Defendants:

The Plaintiff Kuldip and Gateway has been
oppressed and business has been prohibited within the Supreme Court Actions
H-091177 (Conconi Foreclosure Proceeding); S111030 (Manjit alleged oppression
proceeding against Gateway); and S-123329 (Gateway oppression proceeding) (the
“Actions”).

The Plaintiff say when the Courts have been
intentionally deceived by the Lawson Defendants in the Actions then this is not
proper adjudication.  The doctrine of Res judicata in not relevant and the
Supreme Court is not
Functus officio
.

The Plaintiffs say, that if matters had been
adjudicated properly the Mortgage CA881667 would be declared as redeemed
pursuant as a final order of the Court with excess payments made to Conconi
established and returned.

The Plaintiffs say that although the
“Mortgage Redemption” issue is under Appeal.  However, the Court of Appeal is
not a court to hear or correct intentional acts intended to cause delay and
irreparable harm in relief denied intentionally.

The Plaintiffs say that Justice Burnyeat has
either been deceived or is providing partial justice, or is preventing a
serious problem from being exposed, is intentionally biased.

The Plaintiffs say that they have not
received a detailed payout statement to achieve financing and the Defendant
Manjit does not want his funds returned, he wants control.

The Plaintiffs say that the Defendant Manjit
accepted the illegal strategy proposed by the Lawson Defendants with an
intentional strategy to achieve corporate theft with the oppression proceeding
being abused, or he relied on the advice from the Lawson Defendants and was
induced into this litigation for unjust enrichment.

The Lawson Defendants without consequences
or protection from the courts have shamelessly continued with Kuldip’s
character being under attack, is an [sic] character assassination and
defamation.

The Plaintiffs
say that the Defendant Manjit is perhaps unaware of Kuldip’s offer in open
court to have his equal share based on development conditions when the Lawson
Defendants did not stand down to seek instructions from the Defendant Manjit.

[
7
]

In the Action, the Plaintiffs allege against the
Lawson Defendants that they have caused damages to the Plaintiffs by the
following in that:

a.     Manjit was not a shareholder and claims were made without
evidence;

b.     Manjit was not a majority contributor;

c.     Lawson proceeded despite warning letter from the Plaintiff
Gateway;

d.     The Injunction was registered as an abuse of process;

e.     The Injunctions was consented to develop and but no
development has commenced;

f.     The Injunction is a tool to protect the interest of a party
not to prohibit operations or deny the right to refinance that exists within
the foreclosure;

g.     The “other person” or “the Applicant” or “Proper Person” are
all defined terms within the definition of “shareholder” in the
Business
Corporations Act
;

h.     An abuse of the oppression proceeding can cause oppression;

i.      A lawyer as an officer of the court cannot deceive the
court;

j.      A lawyer as an officer of the court cannot alter the
pronounced orders;

k.     The oppression proceeding ought to have terminated but were
not due to protection from the courts in deference granted to officers of the
court;

l.      The oppression proceeding is actually a proceeding to
bankrupt a business or force a share transfer that actually compels a business
to oppress the rightful party;

m.   The litigation was encouraged to be extended and abusive to the
Plaintiffs;

n.     Intended to cause a travesty of justice and an abuse of the
court system;

o.     Claiming that Manjit had no obligation to act in the best
interest of Gateway whilst alleging that Manjit is a shareholder;

p.     In filing a petition without supporting evidence is an abuse
of process;

q.     In interfering with business affairs to generate cash-flow
from revenue properties;

r.     Any other
issues that will be established after discovery.

[
8
]

In the Petition, the Petitioners allege against
the Lawson Defendants as follows:

The Petitioner did not expect that lawyers
at Lawson Lundell LLP would misrepresent the intent of the Injunction, act with
criminal intent, to essentially enjoin and prohibit business operations and
activities.  Further, the Petitioner believed that the ability to vary on two
days’ notice would be a de novo hearing on the merits of the injunction with a
fair adjudication.

On September 20, 2011, the Respondents
filed a Notice of Application to,
inter alia
, vary the injunction to
include those activities that do not deny the Petitioner’s equitable rights in
a foreclosure or affect other statutes or bylaws, such as CRA accounting,
payment of property taxes, etc and for a declaration that the Respondents be
entitled to refinance as permitted by the Order as stated in the reasons by
Justice Burnyeat on October 2011.  These prohibitions in filing an Injunction
constitute oppression on Kuldip and prohibitions on Gateway.

Justice Burnyeat
ordered that Lawson Lundell LLP shall not state in any correspondence with
Gateway that Gateway cannot refinance the mortgage registered on title to the
properties, was ignored. Lawson Lundell LLP’s refused to vary the injunction to
allow for encumbrance on the Properties. These acts are oppressive by Manjit
and his lawyers that are aware that the Conconi Mortgage was redeemed. The
financing was continuously opposed, and this act is oppressive when Manjit is
deemed as the “other person” and “applicant” and is in a position to oppress.

[
9
]

In the Petition, it is alleged that Manjit and the
Lawson Defendants oppressed Kuldip by prohibiting and enjoining Gateway
business operations by:

Manjit and his lawyer’s [sic] at Lawson
Lundell LLP have oppressed Kuldip has prohibited and enjoined Gateway business
operations by:

•

Inducing the foreclosure to take control, rather
than develop.

•

Failing to inform Gateway of the true intent,
deception by his lawyers.

•

Attempting to achieve a Corporate Theft of the
Subject lands.

•

Causing immeasurable pain and suffering to
Kuldip and his family.

•

Having no genuine desire to settle but to
continue with the oppression.

•

Asserting to be shareholder without purchase of
shares in breach of many agreements.

•

Attempting to force a take-over and sabotage the
business.

•

Having no desire to be paid out his funds by
attempting to bankrupt the business.

•

Failing to act in the best interest of Gateway
and Kuldip.

•

Burdening Gateway with higher debt, default
fees, higher interest, etc.

•

Claiming default fees and permitting unjust
enrichment to Conconi and their lawyer.

•

Continuing with a petition that is without merit
and unjust enrichment of his lawyers.

•

Interfering with business affairs to generate
cash-flow from revenue properties.

•

Filing petition without supporting evidence for
unjust enrichment to Manjit.

On February 16, 2011, Manjit served a
Petition with malicious claims, and false statements that is, in itself
oppression.  If Manjit cannot oppress Gateway determined by Justice Burnyeat,
when under the BCA Manjit is not a shareholder classified as the “other
person”, then he had no legal basis to commence the litigation, but in doing
so, and being classified or “tagged’ as a shareholder by his lawyers, Manjit
and his counsel have oppressed the business through an abuse of legal process.

The fact that the petition was filed by
lawyers is egregious results in Manjit being classified or deemed as the “other
person” or the “applicant” under the BCA pursuant to section 227 (2), despite
the fact that Manjit:

•

was not a shareholder or a majority contributor.

•

had breached a number of Agreements, mcI.
January 23rd 2003 Agreement.

•

having agreed to raise funds and then denying
this, has misled Kuldip.

•

had no intention in developing in the realizing
that development costs are high.

•

had no intention to complete designs in failing
to raise funds for design.

•

failed to disclose the source of the funds to
Gateway or Kuldip.

•

having raised funds from investors did not clear
the Mortgage default.

•

did not contribute equally despite numerous
opportunities to do so.

•

Delayed the project and interfered with the
business affairs.

•

Total disregard to Kuldip’s efforts or
involvement.

CLAIMS AGAINST CONCONI, BRIAN C. MARKUS LAW CORPORATION
AND BRIAN C. MARKUS

[
10
]

In both the Petition and the Action, it is
alleged that there were “Bad Faith or Oppressive Acts by Conconi and their
counsel, Brian Markus”.  Those Defendants are referred to by the Plaintiffs as
the “Conconi Defendants” in the Action.  The Conconi Defendants are said to
have caused delay and damages to the Plaintiffs by:

a.     Not discharging the Conconi Mortgage CA881667 and CPL
BB035998 from title;

b.     Not providing Notice to the Plaintiffs before, during or
after transfer of the Mortgage as a party to the foreclosure when the Mortgage
is paid out in full;

c.     Permitted an alleged transfer, alleged assignment or alleged
purchase of the Conconi Mortgage to Defendant to Defendant Manjit declaring
himself as shareholder;

d.     Continually refusing to keep the Plaintiffs informed of the
dealings despite communications earning interest on a Mortgage that is
redeemed;

e.     Fraud before the court in advising Master Taylor that the
Appearance was not filed;

f.     Fraud before the court in advising Master Taylor that Conconi
did not have an obligation to inform “shareholders” but deal with Gateway,
whilst dealing directly and making a deal to receive excess funds from that
alleged shareholder;

g.     Providing a payout statement to the Defendant Manjit that was
not forwarded to the Plaintiff Gateway as borrower and Plaintiff Kuldip as
guarantor;

h.     Defendant Markus providing legal advice to Defendant Manjit
in a conflict;

i.      Defendant Markus acting dishonourably and being abusive to
Plaintiff Kuldip;

j.      Defendant Markus remaining silent on the issue of redemption
and then claiming Res Judicata in subsequent proceedings;

k.     Dealing with counsel for Manjit in the Oppression proceeding
in discussing or sharing notes in breach of the client-privilege to their
clients;

I.      Unjust enrichment in default fees of $2,525 for NSF despite
some defaults paid;

m.   Provided a false demand letters to the Plaintiffs with interest
on amounts not due;

n.     Claimed project disbursements that are not subject to the
Mortgage interest rate or were not paid by Conconi;

o.     Other issues
that will be included after discovery.

[
11
]

In the Petition, the following is alleged as
against Brian C. Markus Law Corporation and Brian C. Markus:

The payment by Manjit to redeem the Conconi
Mortgage which according to Mr. Markus would be made by end of November
2009.  A payout statement was sent to Manjit, whilst contrary to this, Markus
informed the court that the obligations only exist to serve or show the
Mortgages to the owners of the property.

Gateway
attempted to achieve redemption times greater than six months due to Manjit
being overseas but this was not granted by Master Taylor based on submissions
made by Mr. Markus that Manjit will be paying out (redeeming) the
mortgage.

RELIEF SOUGHT AGAINST ALL OF THE APPLICANTS

[
12
]

In the Petition, the Petitioner defined the
Applicants as the “Respondents”.  The relief sought against the Respondents is
set out as follows:

The Respondent,
had commenced legal action with an intentional strategy to deny fair
opportunity to the Petitioner to sell the lands, develop or delay the
development, interfere with business operations, allege fraud against the
Petitioner, and without consequences have continued to deceive the court, in
Kuldip’s character being under attack, is a
character assassination
.

[
13
]

In the Action, the relief sought against the
Applicants is that they be “enjoined and prohibited in interfering with the
Plaintiffs”, that there be “damages resulting from malicious and fraudulent
claims or acts of the Lawson Defendants and the Conconi Defendants to the
Plaintiffs”.

[
14
]

The “Legal Basis” for the relief sought against
the Applicants was stated to be the following:  “Fraud, Misrepresentation,
Unjust Enrichment, Abuse of Legal Process, Contravention of Orders within the
Supreme Court Actions H091177, S111030, and S123329.  In the Law Society of
British Columbia Rules, Character Assassination,
Order Nisi
”.

APPLICATIONS UNDER RULE 9‑5 TO STRIKE OUT
PLEADINGS

[
15
]

Rule 9‑5)(1) of the
Supreme Court
Civil Rules
(formerly Rule 19(24) of the
Rules of Court
)
provides:

At any stage of a proceeding, the court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading, petition
or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d) it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may pronounce judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

(2)  No evidence
is admissible on an application under subrule (1) (a).

[
16
]

The test to be applied to determine whether an
action should be struck out as disclosing no reasonable claim requires a
conclusion that, assuming that the facts as stated or even if amended are true,
those facts disclose no cause of action, the pleadings disclose no arguable
issue, and it is plain and obvious that the claim cannot succeed.  If there is
a chance that the action may succeed, then the Petition and the Action should
be allowed to proceed:
Hunt v. Cary Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959.

[
17
]

In
Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union
,
2006
BCSC 750
, Garson J., as she then was, provided the following summary of
Rule 9‑5 jurisprudence:

In summary, a pleading will be struck out
if:

(a)     the pleadings are unintelligible, confusing and difficult to
understand (
Citizens for Foreign aid Reform
, [
Citizens of Foreign Aid
Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266
(B.C.S.C.) ]);

(b)     the pleadings do not establish a cause of action and do not
advance a claim known in law (
Citizens for Foreign aid Reform
,
supra
);

(c)     the pleadings are without substance in that they are
groundless, fanciful and trifle with the Court's time (
Borsato v. Basra
,
[
2000 BCSC 28 (CanLII)
, [2000] B.C.J. No. 84 (S.C.)])

(d)     the pleadings are not bona fides, are oppressive and are
designed to cause the Defendants anxiety, trouble and expense (
Borsato v.
Basra
,
supra
);

(e)     the action is brought for an improper purpose, particularly
the harassment and oppression of the Defendants (
Ebrahim v. Ebrahim
,

2002 BCSC 466
).

(at
para. 17)

[
18
]

Pursuant to Rule 9‑5, pleadings that
are so prolix and confusing that it is difficult, if not impossible, to understand
the case to be met should also be struck out:
The Owners, Strata Plan
LMS3259 v. Sze Hang Holding Inc.
,
2009 BCSC 473
, at para.
36
.

DISCUSSION AND CASE AUTHORITIES:

[
19
]

It is clear that Kuldip is not satisfied with
the numerous rulings that have been made by the Court.  The Action and the
Petition claim that the submissions of the Applicants and the positions taken
by the Applicants on behalf of their respective clients have resulted in a
number of rulings that are contrary to law and contrary to the submissions made
by and the wishes of Kuldip relating to these matters.  While the Court of
Appeal may agree with Kuldip that the rulings that have been made are contrary
to law and must be overturned, the question which arises is whether the Lawson
Defendants acting on behalf of Manjit and Markus acting on behalf of Conconi
can be found liable in damages to the Petitioners or the Plaintiffs because the
rulings made by the Court have been contrary to the views and submissions of
Kuldip or because the Applicants have acted other than in accordance with the
duties that they owe to the Court and to their clients.

[
20
]

The Petition and the Action claim that Kuldip
and Gateway have been in “oppressed” as a result of the actions of the
Applicants in that they have “intentionally deceived” the Court so that the
matters before the Court have not been “adjudicated properly”, that Manjit has
been subject to the “illegal strategy prepared by the Lawson Defendants”, and
that Kuldip has been subject to “character assassination and defamation”.  It
is alleged against Markus that they were “acting dishonourably and being
abusive to Kuldip” and that, by “sharing notes” with the Lawson Defendants, they
have been in breach of “client-privilege”.

(a)       Is there a Duty of Care to an Opposing Party?

[
21
]

In
Jensen v. MacGregor
(1992),
1992 CanLII 2167 (BC SC)
, 65
B.C.L.R. (2d) 224 (S.C.), Sinclair Prowse J. made this statement regarding
the possibility that a duty of care might be owed to the person adverse to the
client of the lawyer:

Dealing firstly with the claims made by the
Plaintiff, Peter Krogh Jensen on behalf of himself, although he admits that the
Defendants were at all times the lawyers for his wife, and not for himself,
nonetheless he asserts that the Defendants owed him a duty of care, and that
they are therefore liable for the alleged breach of duty and consequential
damage alleged in the pleadings.

Generally speaking, while a lawyer may owe
an ethical duty to the Court to be candid and fair, the only person to whom a
lawyer owes an actionable duty is to his client (
Al-Kandari v. J.R. Brown
& Co
,
[1988] 1 All E.R. 833 (C.A.)
,
Gerrant v. Maskal et al.

(1985),
1985 CanLII 2349 (SK CA)
, 47 R.F.L. (2d)1 (Sask C.A.)).  With respect to that duty, the lawyer
must be competent and diligent (
Hunter v. Greggin et al.
(1986),
1986 CanLII 3076 (SK QB)
, 55 Sask
R. 59 (Sask. Q.B.)). ...

In other circumstances, a lawyer may owe a
duty of care to a non-client claimant when it is clear to both the lawyer and
the claimant that the claimant was relying on the special legal skill and
knowledge of the lawyer, and that the lawyer knew or ought to have known that
the claimant was relying on this skill or knowledge (
Tracy v. Atkins

(1979),
1979 CanLII 760 (BC CA)
, 105 D.L.R. (3d) 632 (B.C.C.A.),
Kamahap v. Chu
(1989),
1989 CanLII 242 (BC CA)
, 40
B.C.L.R. (2d) 288, and
Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd v. Heller and Partners
Ltd.
,
[1964] A.C. 465 (H.L.)
).

In these
instances, a fundamental element is the lawyer's knowledge that the party
(other than the client) is reasonably relying on the lawyer's skill and
knowledge, and is likely to suffer serious loss if the lawyer acts negligently
(
Klingspon v. Ramsay et al.
unreported, January 9, 1985, No. C821075,
Vancouver Registry (B.C.S.C.)).

[
22
]

Throughout, Kuldip was aware that the Lawson
Defendants and the Conconi Defendants were not acting for him, Gateway or Acumar.
There was nothing to suggest that the Lawson Defendants or the Conconi
Defendants owed a duty of care to the Petitioners and/or to the Plaintiffs.  The
parts of the Petition and the Action which rely upon a duty of care being owed to
the Petitioners and the Plaintiffs disclose no reasonable cause of action and are
bound to fail.  I am satisfied that it is plain and obvious these parts of the
Petition and the Action must be struck out as that part of the claim cannot
succeed.

(b)       If Lawyers Mislead the Court

[
23
]

Kuldip makes a number of allegations that the
Applicants have misled and intentionally deceived the Court.  Any obligation
owed to the Court does not result in a breach of duty to the opposing party.
In
Martel v. Andrew
,
2005 ABCA 63 (CanLII)
, [2005] 6 W.W.R. 623 (Alta. C.A.), the Court made
this statement:

The Appellant bases her argument that the
Respondents acted in bad faith on the fact that Mr. Martel swore an
affidavit in which he swore that he had not been served with the Statement of
Claim in the Matrimonial Property Dispute.  The Appellant says this affidavit
was false.  The Respondents relied upon this affidavit while acting for
Mr. Martel to open up a default judgment that the Appellant had previously
obtained.  She alleges that the Respondents presented this affidavit “knowingly
and in bad faith”.  However, she provides no evidence of the alleged knowledge
and bad faith and simply asserts them as facts.  The chambers judge concluded
that whether or not Mr. Martel lied in his affidavit does not translate
into bad faith since there is no duty on counsel presenting an affidavit to
court to verify that the information sworn to is true.

We agree.  Doubtless a lawyer owes a duty to
the court not to offer into evidence an affidavit that he knows to be false or
misleading.  However, that does not mean that a lawyer must believe what his
client swears to; still less does it mean that a lawyer has a duty to
investigate to determine whether or not what his client states to be true is,
in fact, true or false.  Further, the duty to the court is a public duty and
owed as an officer of the court to the court and not a private duty owed to the
opposite side in the lawsuit.  There is ample authority that the duties that a
lawyer owes to the opposing party are viewed very restrictively: German v.
Major (1985),
1985 ABCA 176 (CanLII)
, 62 A.R. 2 (C.A.).  There are good policy reasons for this in the
adversarial system.  If it were otherwise, the conflicting duties owed by a
lawyer would make the adversarial system impossible.

(at
paras. 11-12)

[
24
]

The obligations owed by counsel for Kuldip and
Conconi are not private duties owed to Kuldip, Gateway and Acumar.  If Kuldip
and Gateway are of the belief that the Lawson Defendants and/or the Conconi
Defendants have not fulfilled obligations and duties that they owe the Court,
then any recourse is other than what is set out in the Petition and the Action.

[
25
]

The complaint of the Plaintiffs and the
Petitioners flows from their dissatisfaction with the rulings and orders that
have been made by the Court.  The complaint against the Lawson Defendants is
that they have provided Manjit with an “illegal strategy” and that Manjit has
accepted that strategy.  Even if I could find that there had been a breach of
the duty that counsel owed to the Court, I could not conclude that any such
alleged breach would also result in a breach of duty owed to the Plaintiffs and
the Petitioners.  Having been unsuccessful before the Court in advancing the
theories about the oppression alleged in the Kuldip Oppression Action and in
various applications made before the Court in the Kuldip Oppression Action, in the
Manjit Oppression Action, and in the Foreclosure Action, Kuldip now seeks to
visit that dissatisfaction on the Applicants.

[
26
]

Those parts of the pleadings in the Petition and
in the Action which allege that damages are available because the Applicants
have misled the Court do not advance a claim known at law.  I dismiss those
parts of the Petition and those parts of the Action which purports to seek
damages as a result of alleged “intentional deception” and alleged breaches of
duty owed to the Court by the Lawson Defendants and the Conconi Defendants.  It
is plain and obvious that, even if amended, these claims cannot succeed.

(c)       Did the Applicants Oppress Kuldip?

[
27
]

Claiming pursuant to s. 227 of the
Business
Corporations Act
, the Petitioners and Plaintiffs allege that the Applicants
“oppressed” Kuldip.  That
Act
relates only to those who use their
particular powers in a corporation to oppress others.  Throughout, Kuldip has had
control of Gateway and Acumar so that it would be impossible to conclude that
the Applicants can somehow be brought within the provisions of the
Act
.

[
28
]

On the basis that Manjit never had any effective
control of Gateway, the Kuldip Oppression Action was dismissed as it would not
be possible to conclude that Manjit had used Gateway to oppress Kuldip .  Similarly,
it would not be possible to conclude that the Lawson Defendants acting on
behalf of Manjit could have used Gateway to oppress Kuldip.  If Manjit was not
in a position to use Gateway to oppress Kuldip, it would not have been possible
for the Lawson Defendants to use Gateway to oppress Kuldip.  Rather, they were
merely acting on the instructions of Manjit to commence the Manjit Oppression
Action and to defend the Kuldip Oppression Action.

[
29
]

However, Kuldip goes beyond the provisions of
the
Business Corporations Act
to allege that he has been “oppressed” by
the activities of the Applicants.  I am satisfied that oppression as a civil
remedy is not a claim known at law.  I conclude that any common law action for
“oppression” is bound to fail.

[
30
]

Those parts of the Petition and Action which
allege damages resulting from oppression are struck.  It is plain and obvious
that the claim advanced by Kuldip cannot succeed even if the claims were
amended in order to correct the confusing recitation of what is alleged.

(c)       Claims of Defamation and/or “Character
Assassination”

[
31
]

Any statements made in Court by the Lawson
Defendants in representing Manjit in the Kuldip Oppression Action or in the
Manjit Oppression Action or any statements made in Court by the Conconi
Defendants in the Foreclosure Action are absolutely privileged.  A civil action
does not lie with respect to those statements in any event:
Geyer v. C.C.I.
Merritt
(1977),
1979 CanLII 682 (BC SC)
, 16 B.C.L.R. 27 (S.C.);
Holland v. Douglas
,
[2010]
B.C.J. No. 125 (S.C.)
;
Turner v. Cuttler
,
[1997] B.C.J.
No. 1014 (S.C.)
and
Lawrence v. Sandilands
,
2003 BCSC 211 (CanLII)
, [2003] B.C.J.
No. 343 (S.C.).

[
32
]

To the extent that the claims set out in the
Petition and the Action relate to alleged defamatory statements said to have
been made by the Applicants, the claims are struck out as it is plain and
obvious that they cannot succeed.

(d)       Other Claims Advanced by the Petitioners and the
Plaintiffs.

[
33
]

The Plaintiffs and the Petitioners advance the
proposition that the matters before the Court would have been “adjudicated
properly” but for the representations made by the Lawson Defendants and but for
the “illegal strategy proposed by the Lawson Defendants” and adopted by Manjit.
The Petitioners and the Plaintiffs seem to proceed on the assumption that the
Lawson Defendants are pursuing their own agenda and have not fully advised
Manjit of the submissions that they are making on his behalf to the Court.
While this complaint is raised in the Petition and in the Action, the
Petitioners and the Plaintiffs do not allege a particular cause of action
flowing from these activities by the Lawson Defendants.  Even if the Petition
and the Action was amended to allege facts to support such an alleged cause of
action available to the Plaintiffs and the Petitioners, it is plain and obvious
that any such claim could not succeed.

[
34
]

As against the Conconi Defendants, it is alleged
that they acted “dishonourably” and were “abusive” to Kuldip.  Damages are also
claimed on the basis that a “detailed payout statement” has not been received
by Gateway or Kuldip.  Despite the fact that Gateway and Kuldip have received
an Order of the Court that there be a reference before the Registrar of the
Court to determine balances owing under the Conconi Mortgage, Gateway and/or
Kuldip have not taken steps to set an appointment before the Registrar of the
Court in that regard.  In those circumstances and in view of a previous finding
that a number of payout statements had been provided to Gateway, it would not
be possible to conclude that the damages against the Conconi Defendants could
arise out of an alleged failure to provide a “detailed payout statement”.

[
35
]

To the extent that there are further claims set
out in the Petition in the Action which related to claims against the
Applicants, the claims are struck out as it is plain and obvious that they
cannot succeed.

CONCLUSION REGARDING THE RULE 9‑5 APPLICATION

[
36
]

Pursuant to Rule 9‑5 of the
Supreme
Court Civil Rules
, I find that the Petition and the Notice of Civil Claim
disclose no reasonable claim and that those portions of the Petition and the
Action as they relate to the Applicants must be struck out.

[
37
]

In the circumstances, I am satisfied that the
Applicants are entitled to receive one set of costs against Gateway, Acumar and
Kuldip on a Party and Party (Scale B) basis, payable forthwith after
assessment.

SHOULD AN ORDER BE MADE PURSUANT TO S. 18 OF THE
SUPREME
COURT ACT
?

[
38
]

Section 18
of the
Supreme Court Act

provides:

If, on
application by any person, the court is satisfied that a person has habitually,
persistently and without reasonable grounds, instituted vexatious legal
proceedings in the Supreme Court or in the Provincial Court against the same or
different persons, the court may, after hearing that person or giving him or
her an opportunity to be heard, order that a legal proceeding must not, without
leave of the court, be instituted by that person in any court.

[
39
]

In
Holland v. Douglas
,
2010 BCSC 1560
,
B. Brown J. adopted the following as characteristics of a typical
vexatious proceeding:

In
Lang Michener v. Fabian
(1987)
1987 CanLII 172 (ON HCJ)
, 37
D.L.R. (4th) 685, the Ontario High Court described the characteristics of a
typical vexatious proceeding:

(a)     bringing one or more actions to decide an issue which has
already been determined by a court of competent jurisdiction;

(b)     where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or if the
action would lead to no possible good, or if no reasonable person can
reasonably expect to obtain relief;

(c)     actions brought for an improper purpose, including the
harassment or oppression of other parties by multifarious proceedings brought
for purposes other than the assertion of legitimate rights;

(d)     grounds and issues raised tend to be rolled forward into
subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with actions brought
against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant in earlier
proceedings;

(e)     failure of the person instituting the proceedings to pay the
costs of unsuccessful proceedings;

(f)     persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial
decisions; and

(g)     in determining whether proceedings are vexatious, the court
must look at the whole history of the matter and not just whether there was
originally a good cause of action.

(at
para. 8)

[
40
]

The Applicants point to a number of previous
actions commenced by Kuldip where the lawyers representing those opposed to
Kuldip, Acumar or Gateway were eventually named as defendants.  On April 26,
2011, Kuldip and Acumar commenced S.C.B.C. Action No. 134571 (New
Westminster Registry), in which they named the following lawyers/law firms as
defendants:  Geoff Thiele, Robert W. Hunter, Bull Housser and Tupper LLP,
Janine Stewart, Singleton Urquhart LLP, and Stephen Berezowskyj.  On April 29,
2011, Kuldip and Acumar commenced S.C.B.C. Action No. 134631 (New
Westminster Registry), in which they named the following lawyers/law firms as
defendants: Hoops Harrison, Boughton Law Corporation LLP, Richards and Richards
LLP, George H. Richards, James Lida, Nordel Law LLP, Herbinder Dulay, Kashmir
Gandham and Sukhbinder Nunrha.

[
41
]

The tactics of this Petition and of this Action
have been repeated in other actions.  In
Vancouver City Savings Credit Union
v. Randhawa et al.

[2011] B.C.J. No. 1838 (S.C.)
, Harris J., as
he then was, made this statement in this regard:

... When set against those criteria,
proceedings have been taken habitually or persistently in the absence of
objectively reasonable grounds.  They have been pursued obstinately, despite judicial
criticism and clear statements by other judges of the relevant principles
applicable to the matters before the court.  The respondents have repeatedly
brought matters that have previously been decided back to the court in
circumstances where it is obvious that the application could not succeed.  Those
applications, in the words of Ryan J.A., have been doomed to fail.  The grounds
and issues raised have tended to be rolled forward into subsequent proceedings
where they have been repeated and supplemented.  The proceedings have
improperly attempted to ensnare counsel.  The respondents have failed
responsibly to pursue the procedural avenues open to them to deal with any
legitimate concerns that they have.  All of this is sufficient to justify
concluding that the respondents are vexatious litigants and the order should be
granted.

(at
para. 11)

[
42
]

The claims against the Applicants in the
Petition and the Action merely repeat the complaints that the Petitioners and
the Plaintiffs have raised unsuccessfully in the Kuldip Oppression Action, the
Manjit Oppression Action, and the Foreclosure Action.  The only difference is
that the complaints are now made against the Applicants.

[
43
]

The claims set out in the Petition and in the
Action against the Lawson Defendants and Markus who represented parties adverse
to the interests of the Petitioners and the Plaintiffs is an attempt to disable
these lawyers so that they are not in a position to continue to act for Manjit
or Conconi.  This Petition and this Action are merely an attempt to intimidate
the lawyers who have acted for parties adverse to the Plaintiffs and the
Petitioners and an attempt to further litigate issues which have already been
determined by the Court.

[
44
]

The Action and the Petition have no other
purpose other than to harass and oppress the lawyers for Manjit and Conconi.
The claims in the Action and the Petition are not advanced for the purpose of asserting
legitimate rights.

[
45
]

It appears also to be the case that the
Petitioners and Plaintiffs have failed to pay costs of the unsuccessful
proceedings.  In particular, the Plaintiffs have refused to pay costs ordered
against them in the Foreclosure Action and have refused to pay the costs
associated with the Kuldip Oppression Action which has been dismissed.

[
46
]

To succeed in an application pursuant to

s. 18
of the
Supreme Court Act
, the Applicants must demonstrate
that the Petition and the Action are vexatious in the sense of having been
taken in the absence of objectively reasonable grounds and that proceedings
have been brought habitually or persistently such that the litigant has
continued obstinately in the course of conduct, despite protests or criticism.
I find that the Applicants have been successful in showing that the
pleadings of Kuldip, Gateway and Acumar are vexatious legal proceedings.

[
47
]

I am satisfied that this is an appropriate case
to order that the Plaintiffs and the Petitioners be prohibited from bringing or
commencing proceedings in this Honourable Court against Lawson Lundell LLP,
Craig C. Ferris, Laura Bevan, Kinji Bourchier, Brian C. Markus Law Corporation
and Brian C. Markus without leave of a Justice of the Honourable Court.  The Plaintiffs
and the Petitioners are also prohibited from bringing or commencing proceedings
in this Honourable Court against B.D.M. Loewen or his law firm who have
represented the Applicants in these proceedings.
